name: The Card Payment Lifecycle
intent: A card payment is a chain of separate steps, not one event: authorization holds the funds, capture charges them, a void releases an unused hold, settlement moves the money between banks later, and a refund is a new transaction.
scenario: An online shop takes an order of 100.00 on a card that has 500.00 available. It authorizes the card when the order is placed, captures part of it when the first item ships, lets the rest of the hold expire, and refunds a part later. The provider takes a fee of 2.9% plus 30 cents on each capture and pays the merchant two days after the capture.
problem: Treating "the payment" as one yes-or-no call hides the states in between. A shop that charges at checkout and ships a week later cannot cancel without a refund, a hotel that charges the full amount up front annoys guests, and an order shipped in two parcels needs two charges. Teams also confuse a hold with money: the cardholder's balance dropped, but the merchant has nothing yet, and a hold that is left unused blocks the customer's funds until it expires. Without the model, support cannot answer where the money is, and code accepts actions the card system will refuse.

howItWorks.title: Authorize: ask the issuer to hold the funds
howItWorks.text: The merchant sends the card details (or a token) and an amount through the payment provider, which asks the cardholder's bank, the issuer, whether it will honour that amount. If it agrees, the amount is put on hold: the cardholder's available balance drops, but no money has moved and no charge is final. The result is an authorization that can be captured, voided or left to expire. A decline moves no money and leaves no charge, though some providers bill a small fee per authorization attempt.

howItWorks.title: Capture: turn the hold into a charge
howItWorks.text: When the goods ship or the service is delivered, the merchant captures the authorization. Capture can be for the full amount or for less, for example when only part of an order ships, and it can happen later, but only while the hold lasts. How a partly used hold behaves differs between providers: some release the rest at once, some keep it available for further captures until it expires. A capture is the point where the merchant fee is typically calculated.

howItWorks.title: Void or expire: release what was not used
howItWorks.text: If the order is cancelled before capture, the merchant voids the authorization and the hold is released, so the customer sees their funds again with no charge to reverse. If nobody acts, the hold expires after some days, the limit depending on the card network, the issuer and the type of business, and a capture after that is rejected: the merchant must authorize again, which can fail if the funds are gone.

howItWorks.title: Settle: the money moves between banks, later
howItWorks.text: Captures are collected into batches, and the provider pays the merchant some time afterwards, typically a day or more, and net of fees. Until then the merchant's money is pending: the customer has been charged, but the merchant's bank account has nothing new. Settlement reports are what the merchant matches against its own records, the subject of reconciliation.

howItWorks.title: Refund: a separate transaction after capture
howItWorks.text: A refund returns money after a capture. It is its own transaction, linked to the original, and it cannot exceed what was captured less earlier refunds. It is not an undo: the customer is charged and refunded as two events, the merchant usually pays out of its next settlement, and whether the fee is returned depends on the provider. Before capture the right tool is a void, which leaves no charge at all.

pros: Authorizing first tells the merchant the card is good before goods are shipped
Capturing at shipment charges only for what was delivered, in one or several amounts
A void cancels cleanly: the customer never sees a charge or waits for a refund
Each step is a distinct, recorded event, so support and finance can say where an amount is
cons: More states and more rules to model, and each one can be rejected for its own reason
Holds tie up the customer's funds until they are captured, voided or expire, which customers notice
The merchant gets paid after settlement, so cash flow trails sales by days
Limits (hold duration, partial and repeated capture, fee on refund) differ by provider and card, so they must be read from the provider's documentation
whenToUse: Goods that ship after the order, so the charge should follow the shipment
Services with an uncertain final amount, such as hotels, rentals or fuel, where a hold is adjusted or partly captured
Any system that needs to cancel before charging, rather than charge and refund
whenNotToUse: Instant digital goods, where authorize and capture in one step (a sale) is simpler and the delay buys nothing
Very long gaps between order and delivery, where a hold will expire anyway: take a saved payment method and charge at the time
Other payment methods that do not have a hold step, such as many bank transfers, which have their own states
pitfalls: Capturing after the hold has expired and treating the rejection as a card failure instead of re-authorizing
Refunding when a void is possible, which leaves the customer with a charge and a refund and the merchant with a fee
Letting authorizations pile up unused, so customers see their funds blocked for no reason
Reading a captured payment as money in the bank, when settlement has not happened yet
Assuming the remainder of a partly captured hold stays available, when the provider has released it
Allowing a refund larger than the captured amount in your own code and finding out only from the provider's error

roles.label: Cardholder
roles.description: Pays with a card and sees holds and charges in their available balance.

roles.label: Merchant
roles.description: Authorizes at checkout, captures at shipment and refunds on return.

roles.label: Payment provider
roles.description: Connects the merchant to the card system and pays out after settlement.

roles.label: Issuer
roles.description: The cardholder's bank: approves the authorization and holds the funds.

roles.label: Card network
roles.description: Carries authorization and settlement messages between the banks.

quiz.question: A hotel authorizes 300.00 on a guest's card at check-in, and the guest's banking app shows 300.00 less available. Has the guest been charged?
options: Yes, because the available balance fell, so the money has already moved.
Yes, but the hotel can reverse the charge freely until the guest leaves.
No, it is a hold on funds: the charge happens only at capture, and a void or expiry releases it.
No, because an authorization does not change the available balance at all.
quiz.explanation: Authorization asks the issuer to set the amount aside, which lowers the available balance, but nothing is charged or paid to the merchant. Capture makes the charge, and a void or an expiry gives the funds back. Money moves between banks only at settlement.

quiz.question: A shop authorizes an order and tries to capture it 10 days later. The provider rejects the capture because the hold expired. What should the shop do?
options: Retry the same capture after an hour, as the rejection is probably temporary.
Refund the customer 100.00 to clear the problem, then capture again.
Capture a smaller amount, which is never subject to the expiry limit.
Authorize the card again, which succeeds only if the funds are still available, then capture.
quiz.explanation: An expired hold is gone, so no capture can succeed against it. The merchant needs a new authorization, and the issuer may decline it if the funds are no longer there. Nothing was charged, so there is nothing to refund, and the expiry applies to any amount.

quiz.question: A capture of 100.00 succeeded this morning, but the merchant's bank balance has not changed. Why?
options: The capture failed silently, so the merchant should capture again.
Settlement has not happened yet: the money moves between banks later, typically after a day or more.
The fee has to be paid first, and the merchant is paid only after the fee clears.
Captured money is held by the provider until the customer confirms delivery.
quiz.explanation: Capture charges the cardholder, but the payout to the merchant comes with settlement, typically a day or more later and net of fees. Until then the amount is pending. Capturing again would charge the customer twice.
